'''''James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing''''' is a 2004 [[action adventure game]] developed by [[Visceral Games|EA Redwood Shores]] and published by [[Electronic Arts]] for the [[PlayStation 2]], [[GameCube]], and [[Xbox (console)|Xbox]]. The game features a cast of voice actors including [[Pierce Brosnan]], reprising his film role as MI6 agent [[James Bond]]. Other returning actors include [[Richard Kiel]], [[John Cleese]] and [[Judi Dench]], as [[Jaws (James Bond)|Jaws]], [[Q (James Bond)|Q]] and [[M (James Bond)|M]] respectively, alongside [[Willem Dafoe]], [[Heidi Klum]], [[Misaki Ito]], [[Shannon Elizabeth]], and [[Mýa]]. It is considered a continuation of ''[[Die Another Day]]'' (2002), featuring Brosnan and Cleese in their final performances as Bond and Q, respectively.

Development of the game began in 2001. Written by [[Bruce Feirstein]], [[Danny Bilson]], and [[Paul De Meo]], ''Everything or Nothing'' centers around Bond dealing with the use of [[nanotechnology]] as terrorism. The player controls Bond, and the game includes several driving levels. It is the second Bond game played in third-person after ''[[Tomorrow Never Dies (video game)|Tomorrow Never Dies]]'' (1999), and is the first Bond game to feature a two-player cooperative mode. ''Everything or Nothing'' was released in February 2004. It received "generally positive reviews" according to [[Metacritic]].

==Gameplay==
[[File:JBEON game screenshot.jpg|thumb|left|300px|''Everything or Nothing'' features third-person gameplay and utilizes cover mechanics.]]

The gameplay is an [[action-adventure game]] with a mix of third-person shooting/action sequences and vehicle sequences. In third-person missions, Bond can typically use cover, engage in hand-to-hand combat, use gadgets, and perform some context-sensitive actions, while driving sequences primarily involve racing to a specific objective. The player drives multiple vehicles throughout the game, including the [[Aston Martin Vanquish]], [[Porsche Cayenne Turbo]], a [[Subaru Impreza]] rally car, and a [[Triumph Daytona 600]] motorcycle.<ref name="ps2.ign.com">{{Cite web|url=http://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/18/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing-7|title=James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing (PS2)|last=Mirabella III|first=Fran|website=IGN|date=February 17, 2004|access-date=December 4, 2013|archive-date=December 24, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224212200/http://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/18/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing-7|url-status=live}}</ref> The player can complete objectives in multiple ways, and players are awarded "Bond Moments" when they complete an objective, feat, or task in a manner consistent with Bond's actions in films. These actions frequently involve the use of Bond's gadgets, which include a rappel gun, remote-controlled Q-Spider drones, and a wristwatch equipped with a strobe flash. A diverse arsenal of ranged weapons is available, headlined by Bond's contemporary standard-issue sidearm, the Walther P99.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Everything or Nothing? |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/06/everything-or-nothing-3|website=IGN|access-date=September 22, 2021|date=February 6, 2004|archive-date=April 16, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230416011735/https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/06/everything-or-nothing-3|url-status=live}}</ref>

The game is identical across each console, aside from minor graphical and sound differences. A cooperative mode was included for two players in which two unnamed operatives must complete missions using the same gameplay mechanics as the single-player portion of the game. The [[PlayStation 2]] version included an online version of this mode.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Mirabella|first=Fran |title=James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing Head-to-Head|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/18/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing-head-to-head |website=IGN |access-date=September 22, 2021 |date=February 18, 2004 |archive-date=March 20, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160320184349/http://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/18/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing-head-to-head|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=Casamassina/><ref>{{Cite web|last=Torres|first=Ricardo|title=James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing Online Impressions|url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing-online-impressions/1100-6089036/|website=GameSpot|access-date=September 22, 2021|date=February 6, 2004|archive-date=March 21, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140321164955/http://www.gamespot.com/articles/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing-online-impressions/1100-6089036/|url-status=live}}</ref> Electronic Arts retired the game's servers in January 2006.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ea.com:80/official/007/everythingornothing/us/home.jsp?ncc=1|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060326100610/http://www.ea.com/official/007/everythingornothing/us/home.jsp?ncc=1|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 26, 2006|title=Official Website of EA 007 EON; Archived on March 26, 2006|access-date=May 29, 2018}}</ref> Another version of ''[[James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing (GBA video game)|Everything or Nothing]]'' was published for the [[Game Boy Advance]] and can be linked to the GameCube version via the [[GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable]], providing unique premium content.

==Plot==
The game opens in the [[Pamir Mountains]], [[Tajikistan]], 2004, where [[MI6]] agent James "007" Bond infiltrates a stronghold where an organization sells a stolen [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] [[Suitcase nuclear device|suitcase bomb]]. Bond triggers a firefight between the two factions making the exchange, using the confusion to steal the device and escape.

Following the mission, Bond is briefed on the disappearance of Oxford scientist Dr. Katya Nadanova ([[Heidi Klum]]), who oversees a top-secret [[nanotechnology]] [[Humanitarianism|humanitarian]] project. Bond's search leads to a weapons research facility in [[Egypt]], where he is ordered to rescue Nadanova and prevent the theft of the nanobot prototypes. Destroying the facility, Bond follows the kidnappers onto an [[Armoured train|armored train]] where he encounters and dispatches Jaws (using the likeness of [[Richard Kiel]]). Bond discovers Nadanova and rescues her before pursuing the terrorist via helicopter through the [[Valley of the Kings]]. Bond defeats the terrorist and takes Nadanova to her safehouse, where, after Bond departs, it is revealed that she is working in conjunction with Nikolai Diavolo ([[Willem Dafoe]]), a former [[KGB]] agent who seeks revenge for the death of his mentor and friend [[Max Zorin]] (the primary antagonist of the 1985 film ''[[A View to a Kill]]''). The two intend to repurpose the nanobots for far more sinister purposes than their original intention of repairing nuclear reactors.

Upon returning to MI6, M ([[Judi Dench]]) informs Bond of the disappearance of another 00 agent, Jack Mason, alias 003, who was last seen investigating a platinum mine in [[Peru]]. Bond is sent there to track down Mason's last known contact, Serena St. Germaine ([[Shannon Elizabeth]]), an American [[geologist]] who may have a clue to his whereabouts. Serena takes Bond to a mining complex, where he discovers Mason is being tortured by Diavolo. Before succumbing to his wounds, Mason informs Bond that Diavolo intends to move his operations to [[New Orleans]]. Bond learns of Nadanova's ties with Diavolo when she captures Serena and throws her out of a helicopter. Bond dives off a cliff to rescue her through the use of Q's ([[John Cleese]]) rappel gadget, and the two escape Diavolo's mercenaries via tank.

Searching New Orleans, Bond learns that Diavolo has enlisted a [[War crime|war criminal]] named Arkady Yayakov to help repurpose the nanobots. Bond infiltrates a factory owned by Diavolo and uncovers a lead pointing to a local nightclub owned by Yayakov, where he crosses paths with Mya Starling ([[Mýa]]), an NSA field operative who is also investigating Diavolo. However, Starling's cover is blown, and she is being held in a 19th-century [[cemetery]] by Yayakov, who hands her over to local mobster Jean Le Rouge. Bond and Le Rouge chase through the cemetery while dispatching Yayakov's men, eventually reaching a crematorium until Bond kills Le Rouge and rescues Starling.

Bond tracks Diavolo's operations to an abandoned plantation in Louisiana, where he discovers Diavolo has altered Nadanova's nanobots to eat through all metals but platinum, disintegrating everything they come in contact with. After destroying the laboratory and killing Yayakov, Bond reencounters Jaws, who is driving a tanker truck laden with nanobots across the [[Lake Pontchartrain Causeway]] towards the levees of New Orleans with the intent of flooding the city. Bond disables Jaws' tanker truck, causing him to lose control and plunge into [[Lake Pontchartrain]], averting the threat of destruction in New Orleans, and Bond returns to Peru to investigate Diavolo's platinum mines.

After winning a [[Rallying|rally race]] hosted by Diavolo, Bond finds he has captured Serena, allowing Diavolo to escape to the mines. After saving Serena, Bond reaches the mines but is captured by Nadanova. Diavolo explains that he intends to use the nanobots to destroy the [[Kremlin]] and use his army of tanks, armored with platinum to make them immune to the nanobots, to control Russia and then overthrow Europe. Tied in the path of a mining drill, Bond escapes his shackles and flees the mines in a helicopter piloted by Serena.

Following Diavolo to [[Moscow]], Bond steals one of Diavolo's platinum tanks and uses it to prevent the release of the nanobots in [[Red Square]]. He then heads for a missile silo hidden under the Kremlin, where Bond rappels down a large elevator shaft until being confronted by Nadanova and her men. Bond shoots the elevator brakes, causing it to plummet out of control, confronts a flamethrower-wielding Jaws for the third and final time, defeating him in the process, and escapes the collapsing elevator with the aircraft's ejector seat. After heading to the bunker and deactivating the nanotech missiles while dispatching most of Diavolo's men, Diavolo and Nadanova then attack Bond with a Soviet-era [[Fighter aircraft|fighter jet]] from an adjacent shaft. Bond destroys the jet, killing Nadanova though Diavolo ejects just in time. Diavolo reaches a control tower, reactivating one of the missiles and targeting it at [[London]]. Bond destroys the control tower, where Diavolo managed to launch the missile before plunging to his death into the silo. By destroying the missile as it launches, Bond prevents the catastrophe and reunites with Serena outside the Kremlin.

The game's third-person perspective was a change from the first-person view typically used in earlier Bond games.<ref name=Mirabella>{{Cite web|last=Mirabella|first=Fran|title=E3 2003: James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2003/05/08/e3-2003-james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing|website=IGN|access-date=September 22, 2021|date=May 8, 2003|archive-date=April 16, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230416011745/https://www.ign.com/articles/2003/05/08/e3-2003-james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing |url-status=live }}</ref> Game producer Scott Bandy said "we figure that to be Bond, you've got to see Bond. We felt that the first-person perspective, although exciting, didn't put Bond's full potential in the hands of the player. Bond's hand-to-hand fighting style, for example, is almost completely absent in a first-person experience. Bond also fights smart, using cover and corners to his advantage, and third-person is a much better place for that kind of gameplay".<ref name=Q&A/>

|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230416015144/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/bond-everything-or-nothing-goes-gold/1100-6087218/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Bond Goes Gold|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/01/31/bond-goes-gold|website=IGN|access-date=September 22, 2021|date=January 30, 2004}}</ref> and began shipping to U.S. retailers on February 17,<ref>{{Cite web|last=Adams|first=David|title=Everything or Nothing Ships |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/17/everything-or-nothing-ships|website=IGN|access-date=September 22, 2021|date=February 17, 2004|archive-date=April 16, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140416005328/http://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/17/everything-or-nothing-ships|url-status=live }}</ref> with release expected within two days.<ref name=Feldman/> It was released in the U.K. on February 27, 2004.<ref>{{Cite news|last=McGreevey|first=Neil|title=Bond game aims for everything |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/technology/3490944.stm |access-date=September 22, 2021|work=BBC|date=February 27, 2004|archive-date=April 11, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210411005241/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/technology/3490944.stm|url-status=live}}</ref> It was one of the first video games to undergo [[THX]]'s audio certification process.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Moseley|first=Bob|title=EA teams with THX|url=http://www.gamespot.com/gamecube/action/007nothing/news_6076207.html|website=GameSpot|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050122125444/http://www.gamespot.com/gamecube/action/007nothing/news_6076207.html|archive-date=January 22, 2005|date=September 30, 2003}}</ref>

''James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing'' received "generally positive" reviews, according to [[review aggregator]] [[Metacritic]].<ref name="MCGC"/><ref name="MCPS2"/><ref name="MCXBOX"/> ''[[GameSpot]]'' called it "a really great game, perhaps the best James Bond game ever made".<ref name="GSpot" /> ''GameSpot'' later named it the best PlayStation 2 game of February 2004,<ref name=gotm>{{Cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040904091730/http://www.gamespot.com/features/6090209/index.html| url=http://www.gamespot.com/features/6090209/index.html|title=''GameSpot''{{'}}s Month in Review for February 2004|date=March 2, 2004|author=Staff|work=[[GameSpot]]|archive-date=September 4, 2004|url-status=dead}}</ref> and it was a runner-up for the publication's annual "Best Game Based on a TV or Film Property" award.<ref name=bestworst2004>{{Cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050307021607/http://www.gamespot.com/gamespot/features/all/bestof2004/|url=http://www.gamespot.com/gamespot/features/all/bestof2004/|title=Best and Worst of 2004|author=GameSpot|date=January 5, 2005|work=[[GameSpot]]|archive-date=March 7, 2005|url-status=dead}}</ref> ''[[IGN]]'' named it the Game of the Month for February 2004.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Game of the Month: February 2004|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/27/game-of-the-month-february-2004-2|website=IGN |access-date=September 22, 2021|date=February 27, 2004|archive-date=September 22, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200922025744/https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/27/game-of-the-month-february-2004-2|url-status=live}}</ref> ''IGN'' said "EA shakes things up and gives us a fresh new perspective on how good Bond can be."<ref name="ps2.ign.com"/> The game achieved [[Platinum Hits]] status on the Xbox, selling more than two million copies on the Microsoft's console.

Not all critics were as impressed. UK gaming magazine ''[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]]'' stated, "It's perhaps because the title benefits from such a high production spend, in fact, that the average design and execution becomes more pronounced."<ref name="Edge" />

''[[Maxim (magazine)|Maxim]]'' gave it a perfect ten and stated that players can "race through a shitstorm of artillery fire in a Porsche Cayenne Turbo (complete with "Q-cloak" invisibility feature) or missile-firing Triumph Daytona 600."<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=http://www.maxim.com/gaming/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing|title=James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing|last=Porter|first=Alex|magazine=[[Maxim (magazine)|Maxim]]|date=February 17, 2004|access-date=December 4, 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20131204234724/http://www.maxim.com/gaming/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing|archive-date=December 4, 2013}}</ref> ''[[The Times]]'' gave it all five stars and stated that "the over-the-shoulder style does allow for the seamless integration of glossy scenes to drive on the plot and add a more genuine movie-like feel to the game."<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/article/0,,7947-1008770,00.html |title=James Bond: Everything or Nothing |last=Wapshott |first=Tim |newspaper=[[The Times]] |date=February 21, 2004 |access-date=December 4, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060109102831/http://www.timesonline.co.uk/article/0%2C%2C7947-1008770%2C00.html |archive-date=January 9, 2006 |url-status=dead }}</ref> ''[[The Cincinnati Enquirer]]'' gave it four-and-a-half stars out of five and called it "An ambitious but successful interactive adventure that blurs the lines between motion pictures and video games."<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.cincinnati.com/freetime/games/reviews/030404_bond.html|title=Bond title scores with cinema styling|last=Saltzman|first=Marc|newspaper=[[The Cincinnati Enquirer]]|date=March 4, 2004|access-date=December 4, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080509101344/http://www.cincinnati.com/freetime/games/reviews/030404_bond.html|archive-date=May 9, 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref> ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' wrote, "Action addicts still get their share of mayhem, however, as ''EON'' delivers some spectacular levels, including a breakneck highway chase on a flamethrower-equipped motorcycle. Her Majesty would definitely approve."<ref>{{Cite magazine|last=Eng Walk|first=Gary|title=James Bond 007: Everything Or Nothing |url=https://ew.com/article/2004/02/13/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing/ |access-date=September 22, 2021 |magazine=Entertainment Weekly|date=February 13, 2004|archive-date=July 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210725212153/https://ew.com/article/2004/02/13/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing/ |url-status=live }}</ref> ''[[The Village Voice]]'' wrote, "The seamless action—now presented in third person—is spit-shined and ever shifting."<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.villagevoice.com/2004-02-24/news/pierce-n-pussy-galore-in-smoke-and-fuck-free-james-bond/|title=Pierce 'n' Pussy Galore in smoke- and fuck-free James Bond|last=Catucci|first=Nick|newspaper=[[The Village Voice]]|date=February 24, 2004|access-date=December 4, 2013|archive-date=July 27, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100727083823/http://www.villagevoice.com/2004-02-24/news/pierce-n-pussy-galore-in-smoke-and-fuck-free-james-bond/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2008, Anthony Burch of [[Destructoid]] compared the game to a "bad Bond film" such as ''[[Tomorrow Never Dies]]'' or ''[[The World Is Not Enough]]'', citing its mix of "ridiculously bombastic car chases, complete lack of subtlety, and clever cinematic presentation". He was critical of the controls and believed that ''Everything or Nothing'', like previous Bond games, had failed to live up to the success of ''[[GoldenEye 007 (1997 video game)|GoldenEye]]'' (1997). He considered it "halfway decent" when judged on its own.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Burch|first=Anthony|title=Games time forgot: James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing |url=https://www.destructoid.com/games-time-forgot-james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing/|website=Destructoid|access-date=September 22, 2021|date=February 26, 2008|archive-date=September 22, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210922152333/https://www.destructoid.com/games-time-forgot-james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing/ |url-status=live}}</ref> In 2015, Dan Griliopoulos of ''[[TechRadar]]'' ranked it as the second best Bond game of all time, behind ''GoldenEye''.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Griliopoulos|first=Dan|title=The 10 best James Bond games of all time |url=https://www.techradar.com/sg/news/gaming/the-10-best-james-bond-games-of-all-time-1307511|website=TechRadar|access-date=September 22, 2021|date=October 26, 2015|archive-date=January 27, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210127151140/https://www.techradar.com/sg/news/gaming/the-10-best-james-bond-games-of-all-time-1307511 |url-status=live }}</ref>
